title: KV access phase-shift and prefetch adaptation (wip)
content:
Status: exploratory notes, replay-driven profiling and short lab runs. High-level goal: find practical prefetch+eviction adaptors that reduce eviction churn and NVMe/DRAM tail under sudden workload phase shifts (e.g., cold-to-hot hotkey storms, model switch events).

Top-level hypothesis:
- Prefetch predictors tuned for a steady-state hotset react poorly when the working set rapidly shifts (phase-shift). This misalignment produces three correlated effects: (1) transient large-scale prefetching that saturates memory channels and NVMe, (2) eviction churn where recently-prefetched pages are immediately evicted by new arrivals, and (3) reuse-rate collapse for the expected hotset.
- A short-lived adaptive decay on prefetch aggressiveness plus a small hotset-stabilization window should reduce bandwidth spikes and lower spillback without materially increasing long-tail latency.

What I ran (methodology):
- Replayed 24h access traces (prod-sample-2024-09-03) using our trace-replay harness (replayer-v2). Two scenarios: (A) sudden phase shift: 60s cold->hot swap for 10% of keys; (B) gradual drift: same keys ramp over 10 minutes.
- Bench hardware: p4d-like instance image (8x A100 sim), NVMe-backed spill path (3x1.6TB), DDR4 profile. Controlled kernel prefetch disabled to isolate runtime prefetch.
- Telemetry: per-page residency, per-key access inter-arrival (IAT), per-page prefetch timestamps, eviction reason tags, DRAM channel utilization (perf + bpftrace), NVMe io latency histogram (iostat pulses), and per-request tail p50/p95/p99 for token generation.
- Tools: bpftrace scripts for DMA stalls, custom nvprof wrapper for kernel timelines, and ephemeral flamegraphs for CPU-side prefetch thread stalls.

Key observations (raw, unpolished):
1) Bandwidth spikes aligned to phase-shift boundary. In scenario A, aggregate memory channel utilization jumped by ~3.1x for 8s after the swap. NVMe write bursts also increased 4x as prefetch spilled back concurrent with evictions.
2) Prefetch predictor confidence (predictor.confidence score) rose as the predictor observed repeated new-key patterns, but decay was slow (half-life ~45s). That slow decay produced a prefetch tail that outlived the actual hot window, causing overfetch and eviction.
3) Eviction churn metric (evicted_pages/sec) peaked 2x higher than baseline and stayed elevated for 60–120s. Many evicted pages had age < 5s (i.e., prefetched then evicted) => clear sign of wasted bandwidth.
4) Reuse rate collapse: for the intended hotset, measured reuse_rate dropped from 82% to 41% in the 30s after the shift (scenario A). Some of that is genuine (different keys became hot), but a large fraction is due to prefetch/eviction miscoordination.
5) Tail latency impact: p99 token latency rose by 25–40 ms during the bandwidth spike window. Not catastrophic alone, but when combined with multi-tenant interference it pushed a subset of requests over SLO.

Representative flamegraph notes:
- Prefetch worker threads had a blocked->wake pattern caused by memory-channel backpressure (bpftrace showed dma queue stalls when channel util > 85%). CPU spent cycles marshalling prefetch I/O and waiting on io_submit.
- Eviction path spent more cycles in page-list maintenance and reclaimer scans; these are single-threaded locks in current implementation — a hotspot to fix if we want to allow higher asynchronous eviction rates without blocking generation.

Micro-experiments (short, 30–90s each) tried during lab runs:
A) Aggressive-decay experiment: reduce predictor half-life from 45s -> 8s. Result: prefetch volume after phase shift reduced by ~62%, eviction churn down ~48%, but cold-miss rate increased for short-lived sub-hot keys (p50 generation latency +6ms).
B) Stabilization window: add a 5s stabilization window where hotset decisions are withheld from triggering full prefetch until repeat accesses cross a separate 'stability' counter. Result: bandwidth spike amplitude reduced by ~40% and p99 latency improved vs baseline, with negligible effect on steady-state throughput.
C) Throttle-by-bandwidth: dynamic cap that pauses prefetching when DRAM channel utilization > 80%. Result: very effective at limiting NVMe/write-burst but introduced oscillation at high concurrency (prefetch toggles on/off every 1–2s). Needs hysteresis.

Interpretation / tradeoffs:
- Fast-decay alone reduces wasted prefetch but can hurt true hotset warming for short but important bursts (leaderboard-type workloads).
- Stabilization window (small positive delay before heavy prefetching) appears to be a low-cost win: it prevents single-burst noise from causing huge fetch storms while still allowing prefetch for repeat-access keys.
- Bandwidth-aware throttle is necessary for multi-tenant safety but must be smoothed (hysteresis + pid-style controller) to avoid oscillation.
- Eviction path lock contention contributes to CPU-side tail when churn increases. If we reduce lock contention (shard eviction lists or background lockless reclaim), we avoid CPU amplification of the bandwidth problem.

Concrete recommendations (short-term / lab deploy):
1) Prototype stabilization window: implement in predictor daemon a 3–6s default stabilization counter that requires N repeats (configurable, start with 2 repeats). Put behind a runtime flag for 1-week lab rollout.
2) Add a simple exponential decay param per-model (configurable): default half-life 10s for transient-heavy models (chatty retrieval), 60s for steady-state large-batch customers. Expose via model-config.
3) Implement bandwidth cap with hysteresis: pause prefetch when channel_util > 80% and resume when < 65%. Start in observability-only mode (emit events) for two days, then allow enforcement in lab clusters.
4) Micro-optim: split eviction list into 8 shards to reduce lock contention. Run unit perf tests before deploy.

Open questions / TODOs:
- What is the right stability counter vs. half-life mix for retrieval-style loads vs. streaming chat? Need per-workload matrix.
- What's the user-visible impact on cold-start UX for short hot windows if we adopt stabilization? Need A/B with synthetic real-world traffic.
- Can we make the predictor observe per-batch access correlation (i.e., prefer prefetch when batch-locality high)? That could reduce cross-tenant noise.
- Evaluate cost: reduced prefetch means more cold misses hitting NVMe — calc expected token-cost delta for a typical enterprise customer.

Planned experiments (next steps):
- Run A/B on two clusters for 48h: baseline vs. stabilization-window + half-life=10s. Capture p50/p95/p99, eviction churn, NVMe write volume, and cost estimator.
- Replay more traces with different phase-shift magnitudes (1%, 10%, 40% of keys shifting) to map nonlinearity.
- Run microbench where eviction list is sharded to measure CPU tail reduction.

Notes to self / lab pointers:
- Replay harness flags used: --preserve-timestamp --prefetch-emulation=on --trace-filter=phase-shift-only
- Saved traces: s3://redwood-traces/prod-sample-2024-09-03-phaseA.replay.gz (used for scenario A)
- bpftrace snippets: /ops/profiling/bpf/dma-stalls.bt (capture queue depth and blocking timestamps)

Slack/context links: posted preliminary results in #serving-runtime on Nov 13; PR with stabilization proto is here: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/4123 (WIP). JIRA ticket tracking rollouts: JIRA-RT-987.

Quick summary for PM/Eng leadership (one-liner): small stabilization window + faster predictor decay + bandwidth hysteresis reduce transient prefetch storms and eviction churn, cutting NVMe/DRAM spikes and p99 latency during rapid workload phase shifts with minimal steady-state impact.

Appendix (quick stats excerpt):
- baseline eviction_churn_peak: 182 evicted_pages/sec; after stabilization: 98 eps
- peak DRAM channel util (baseline): 89%; after throttle+hysteresis sim: 66%
- reuse rate for intended-hotset (30s window) baseline: 82%; after naive fast-decay: 68% (regained to 79% with stabilization window)

Unresolved: decide config defaults (stabilization window length, stability repeats, decay half-life) and which models get aggressive defaults.

End of notes.

-- Aisha
